newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian cocaine king gets more jail time.
newsitem.headline: Colombian cocaine king gets more jail time.

text.p: Colombian cocaine king Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, who was handed an extremely light prison sentence for crimes he confessed to last month, was sentenced to 22 years in jail on Saturday for a drug shipment he failed to own up to, local media reports said.
National radio and television reports said the sentence was handed down by a "faceless" judge in Bogota who was reported to have been offered a $1 million bribe to let Rodriguez off the hook.

Miguel Rodriguez and his older brother, Gilberto, are self- confessed leaders of the Cali cartel, the billionaire Colombian drug mob that once controlled up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade.

An anonymous judge in Cali sentenced the brothers to lightweight sentences on Jan. 17 that could see them walk free in as little as five years -- because they confessed to certain crimes and because an elaborate plea-bargaining system would cut their assigned prison time substantially.
The 22-year sentence handed down on Saturday means that Rodriguez will serve at least 15 years in prison, however, since it involved a case he repeatedly refused to accept the blame for.
The case involves 330 pounds (150 kg) of cocaine that were smuggled through Costa Rica to Tampa, Fla. in 1989.
Colombia has special tribunals of anonymous or faceless judges as a security measure to protect them against assassination attempts or intimidation by criminal drug gangs.

Judicial officials could not be reached for immediate comment on Saturday's sentence but the same judge who reportedly handed it down could conceivably add additional time to the 22-year sentence if Rodriguez is convicted on a separate charge of trying to bribe him.

Colombia's Congress approved a stiff increase in penalties for drug trafficking earlier this week, increasing the maximum jail sentence from 24 to 60 years. But the sentencing law cannot be applied retroactively and has not yet been signed into effect by President Ernesto Samper.
